//recolor: The manuscript colours seven of its 'Specific Competence(s):' lines green and leaves the other thirteen in the body colour, and it colours the word COPYRIGHT on the imprint page green too. Twenty topic openers that are otherwise identical therefore print two different ways, and the green is the minority. Nothing in this book uses colour to carry meaning — those are the only coloured runs in it — so every author colour is returned to the body colour and the competence line reads the same on every topic opener. The entry carries no 'from', which clears them all: naming one green was not enough, because the manuscript uses two (#92D050 and #00B050) and clearing only the commoner one left four runs behind for the engine's uniform-colour pass to settle on the other green instead. That pass cannot fix this by itself — it compares one colour against another, and here the majority of the same element carries no colour at all. Only runs the author coloured are affected; the theme's own colours are applied at render time and are untouched.
//retext: Two whole-run fixes, kept as retext rather than subtext because the text they match also occurs elsewhere ALREADY CORRECT and must not be touched there. 'What are the learners doing' is asked twenty-four times in this book; twenty-three carry their question mark and one, in Topic 4, does not. 'Different cleaning items help us to keep rooms clean' ends Topic 4's opening prose with no full stop while the two sentences above it have one. A third: "Demonstrate how to use" introduces a list of utensils in Topic 3 and a list of playground equipment in Topic 11, and only the second carries the colon the construction needs. It is a retext rather than a subtext precisely because the other instance is already right — a substring rule would hand that one a second colon.

//subtext: Manuscript slips, each occurring exactly once in the book and each verified against the raw OOXML before being corrected here rather than guessed at from the rendered page. They divide into four kinds. QUESTIONS MISSING THEIR MARK: four questions in LET'S TALK AND LEARN lists end with nothing, or with a full stop, while every one of their siblings in the same list ends with a question mark. WORDS RUN TOGETHER: the manuscript breaks three phrases into separate Word runs with no space between them, so they print glued — 'Do'/'the'/'following:' prints as 'Dothe following:', the option 'c)' is welded to the end of the option before it, and item 5's number is welded to its first word. TYPOS: 'cplour' for 'colour', and 'devise' for 'device' twice in Topic 9 (the same two sentences name the thing correctly elsewhere on the page). A STRAY WORD: activity 3 of Topic 2 is titled '…Showing Various Activities Show', the last word left over from an earlier wording. A MISSING BOX LABEL: Topic 3's Kitchen Utensils section runs one activity in two parts, and the author typed the first as 'LEARNING ACTIVITY 2:  (i) Cleaning Kitchen Utensils' but the second as a bare '(ii) Storing Kitchen Utensils in Suitable Places'. Without the label the engine cannot see the second half as an activity at all, so (i) printed inside the teal activity box and (ii) as an ordinary black heading — the same element, two looks, three inches apart. Restoring the label the author dropped boxes it like its own first half; both halves keep the number 2, which is the manuscript's own scheme (one activity, parts i and ii) rather than a renumbering of the topic. AN INSTRUCTION LEFT IN THE TEXT: Topic 3's Learning Activity 2 heads its look-and-discuss section 'LET'S LOOK (swap the pictures)' — a note to whoever typesets the book, not words for a Grade 1 learner, and it printed as part of the heading. Only the parenthetical is removed here; the picture swap it asks for is a separate change to the artwork itself. A MISTYPED HOUSE HEADING: the book's recurring discuss-the-picture heading is 'LET'S TALK AND LEARN' fifty-six times and 'LET'S TALK AND TALK' twice, both of those followed by the same run of discussion questions as the other fifty-six — the same element, two spellings. Matched on 'TALK AND TALK' rather than on the whole heading because the apostrophe is normalised to a curly one before an override is applied, and that fragment occurs nowhere else in the book. Three further headings read a bare 'LET'S TALK' and are deliberately NOT corrected here: shortening a heading is an editorial choice about the author's wording rather than a typo, and it is left for a human to settle. TWO MIS-NUMBERED ACTIVITIES, each settled against the manuscript's OWN pattern rather than against a house rule. Topic 2 runs its four sections as Activity 1/Exercise 1, 2/2, 3/3 and then 3/4 — the exercises number straight through to four, so the fourth activity is a 4 and the repeated 3 is a slip. Topic 4 runs 1/1, 2/2, 1/3 and 4/4 — the LAST activity is already numbered 4, which only follows if the third is 3, so the stray 1 is the slip. Both are matched on a fragment carrying the number and the first word of the title, which is unique in each case; the second keeps the manuscript's double space after the colon because an override is applied before box titles are normalised. Topic 3 is NOT touched: its 1,2,3 then 1,2(i),2(ii) restarts the count at each sub-topic, which is that topic's own scheme and is internally consistent. A SECOND ROUND of slips, found by reading the whole book rather than any one page, and each verified against the manuscript before being corrected here. MISSING WORDS: Topic 3's opening line reads "tools we use make different things" and Topic 3's third discussion question "Which tools have used before and how did use them?", both of which drop the word that makes the sentence grammatical; Topic 4's exercise asks the learner to "Draw any item you am make from leather", where "am" stands in for "can". MISSPELLINGS: Topic 3 offers "Hummer" as a simple tool (the book spells the action "hammering" elsewhere, and a hammer, not a stove, is the answer the question wants); Topic 4 offers "A lay pot" among things made from clay, two lines under "what can be made from clay"; and Topic 8 spells "welcome" as "welome" twice while spelling it correctly a third time on the same page — the entry carries the bare word so BOTH occurrences are corrected, since a spelling that is right in one line of a page and wrong in the next is exactly the kind of disagreement these corrections exist to remove. Topic 8 also lists the three polite phrases as "please, than you, you are welome", where "than you" is "thank you". SPACING: Topic 4's exercise ends "one way of conserving trees .", with a space before the full stop that no other sentence in the book has. Three more WORDS RUN TOGETHER, of the same kind as the three already listed above and found the same way: the second option of a two-choice question is welded to the end of the first, so the book prints "Thieves(b) visitors", "Volume button(b) power button" and "animals(b) stories" while its six other two-choice questions space the option marker off properly. A THIRD ROUND, from reading the book’s prose end to end rather than from any automated check — the engine’s prose checker is narrow by design and found none of these. MISSPELLINGS: the contents page heads a section "KEY COMPETENCES TO BE DEVELOVED"; Topic 3 asks which tool matches the "pealed" fruit; Topic 8 says to "Clean the widows and window sills"; and Topic 13 asks for a drawing of children playing a "conversional" game, a word the same topic spells "conventional" twice. GRAMMAR: "Being kind to ____ makes them to feel welcome" carries a "to" that the make-someone-do construction does not take; "Which cleaning item have you use?" wants "used"; and the front matter’s rule "Keep your materials safely." sits in a list of three whose siblings take an adjective ("Keep your work area clean"). PARALLELISM: Topic 4’s three instructions run "(a) Plant a tree (b) Reuse a material (c) Collecting waste for recycling", the third breaking the imperative the first two set. PUNCTUATION: "Draw the following utensils;" introduces a list and wants a colon. AND AN INSTRUCTION LEFT IN THE TEXT: an exercise question ends "Match each hand tool to the correct use. (insert a Picture)" — a note to whoever typesets the book, not words for a Grade 1 learner, and the second of its kind here after Topic 3’s "(swap the pictures)". The same PARALLELISM break runs through Topic 8’s cleaning list too: of its seven instructions, five are imperative ("Remove the cobwebs", "Clean…", "Wipe…", "Make the beds", "Arrange chairs") and two are gerunds ("Sweeping the floor", "Collecting litter"), so the two outliers are brought into the list’s own majority form rather than the other way round. The windows entry carries the full stop its six siblings all have. The list-introducing semicolon occurs twice, not once — "Draw the following utensils;" and "Wash the following utensils;" — and both take a colon. The hammer is misspelt TWICE, not once: "(b) Hummer" among the options, and a lowercase "hummer" in the two-cell table of EXERCISE 3, whose sibling cell reads "Adze" — so the table cell takes the capital its neighbour has. The first entry is case-sensitive and did not reach the second. A FOURTH ROUND, prompted by a question about printed page 10 and then extended into a reading of every paragraph in the DOCX itself rather than the markdown by-product. THE PAGE-10 LINE IS THE MANUSCRIPT, NOT THE ENGINE: the docx holds "With your teacher go the nearest road;" as a SINGLE run, so there is no run boundary for the importer to have dropped a word at, and the same instruction four pages earlier reads "With your teacher go to the playground;" — so the book's own wording supplies the missing "to". MORE MISSING WORDS: "cross if there no cars coming" wants "there are no cars". BRITISH ENGLISH THE ENGINE DELIBERATELY WILL NOT TOUCH: Topic 7's competence reads "Practice simple plays", where practise is the verb — the engine leaves the practice/practise pair alone on purpose, because the American spelling is the British NOUN, and this is exactly the judgement it hands to a human; Topic 4's own competence line spells it "Practise ways of conserving materials". CONSISTENCY WITH SIBLINGS: an instruction begins lower-case, "store the following correctly:", where every other instruction in the book is capitalised; "(a) Books, crayons and Pencils." capitalises the third item and not the second; and "from one place to another is a____" glues the article to its blank while the line two above it writes "is a ____". The "conserving trees ." entry was dropped once the engine began settling that space itself: the line prints as "conserving trees." with the entry gone, so it only made the build log report a miss.

//coverImage: The cover hero. The picture the manuscript itself put on the cover showed four learners, none of them with a visible disability, which the house rule requires wherever human beings appear, covers included. This replacement shows six: three boys and three girls, so the gender count is even, and three of them carry a disability between them — an albino learner, a wheelchair user, and a girl wearing a hearing aid. What they are doing is the book’s own subject: drawing, colouring, building with blocks, and writing, in a classroom whose chalkboard and bookshelf say the same. The source picture is a full portrait cover graphic with its own decorative bands top and bottom and a row of topic vignettes below the table; the grade3 cover frames its hero in a 138x82mm landscape window with fit: "cover", so the whole portrait would have been cropped to a thin horizontal slice through the middle, cutting every head off. Only the photograph is used, cropped to exactly that window’s 138:82 so the frame trims nothing further, chosen to clear the Zambian flag above and to leave the standing girl’s hair whole. It is then taken through Real-ESRGAN to 1679px, which is 309 DPI at 138mm.
